claim: Amigo2-icreERT2 mice crossed with Cre-dependent tdTomato reporter mice and treated with tamoxifen showed robust expression of tdTomato in CA2.
source: When crossed with a Cre-dependent tdTomato reporter mouse line (Madisen et al., 2010), we observed robust expression of tdTomato in CA2 of brain sections from Amigo2-icreERT2+; ROSA-tdTomato± mice treated with tamoxifen (Figure 1A–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing tdTomato expression in CA2 after tamoxifen treatment, as shown in Figure 1A-E.

claim: 91.4% of tdTomato-expressing neurons colocalized with the CA2 pyramidal cell marker PCP4.
source: Expression of tdTomato colocalized with the CA2 pyramidal cell marker, PCP4 (Kohara et al., 2014), in 91.4% of neurons (N = 6 mice, Figure 1A,B,E)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative colocalization data from 6 mice and referenced to Kohara et al., 2014 for PCP4 as a CA2 marker.

claim: tdTomato expression colocalized with CaMKIIα, a marker of hippocampal pyramidal neurons.
source: tdTomato colocalized with a marker of hippocampal pyramidal neurons (N = 6; Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing colocalization with CaMKIIα in 6 mice, as shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: tdTomato expression did not colocalize with GAD, a marker of inhibitory neurons.
source: tdTomato colocalized with a marker of hippocampal pyramidal neurons (N = 6; Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) but not inhibitory neurons (N = 3; Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing lack of colocalization with GAD in 3 mice, as shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Amigo2-icreERT2+; ROSA-tdTomato± animals treated with corn oil (tamoxifen vehicle) showed no tdTomato expression.
source: In control experiments, Amigo2-icreERT2+; ROSA-tdTomato± animals treated with corn oil (the tamoxifen vehicle) showed no tdTomato expression (N = 3; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by control experimental data from 3 mice showing no tdTomato expression without tamoxifen treatment.

claim: Infusion of AAVs encoding Cre-dependent hM3Dq or hM4Di into Amigo2-icreERT2+ mice allowed for selective expression of mCherry-DREADD in CA2 pyramidal neurons.
source: Infusion of AAVs encoding Cre-dependent hM3Dq (Figure 1F–H,J) or hM4Di (Figure 1I) with the neuron-specific human synapsin promoter into Amigo2-icreERT2+ mice allowed for selective expression of mCherry-DREADD in CA2 pyramidal neurons without expression in fasciola cinerea, outside of the hippocampus, or in the vasculature, as detected by co-expression of mCherry with PCP4 (N = 4; Figure 1F–G,J).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing selective mCherry-DREADD expression in CA2 pyramidal neurons in 4 mice, as shown in Figures 1F-J.

claim: mCherry expression colocalized with CaMKIIα but not GAD in Amigo2-icreERT2+ mice infused with DREADD AAV.
source: Expression of mCherry also colocalized with the pyramidal cell marker, CaMKIIα (N = 4; Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), but not the interneuron marker, glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD), in GAD-eGFP+; Amigo2-icreERT2+ mice (N = 4; Figure 1I, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from 4 mice showing colocalization with CaMKIIα but not GAD.

claim: In control Amigo2-icreERT2- mice infused with hM3Dq AAV, mCherry expression was absent.
source: In control Amigo2-icreERT2- mice infused with hM3Dq AAV, mCherry expression was absent (N = 4; Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by control experimental data from 4 Cre-negative mice showing no mCherry expression.

claim: CNO treatment dose-dependently increased the firing rate of CA2/proximal CA1 pyramidal neurons in hM3Dq-expressing mice.
source: To confirm that hM3Dq increased neuronal activity, single-unit firing rate was measured from CA2/proximal CA1 pyramidal neurons. Clozapine-N-oxide (CNO) treatment dose-dependently increased the firing rate of pyramidal neurons following CNO administration (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-unit recording data showing dose-dependent increases in firing rate, as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: CNO administration significantly increased hippocampal low-gamma power during running in hM3Dq-expressing Amigo2-icreERT2+ mice at all doses tested (0.5, 1, 2, and 4 mg/kg).
source: We found a significant increase in low-gamma power following CNO administration during running for all doses tested (N = 8; F(1.904, 13.33) = 9.457, p = 0.0030, repeated-measures one-way ANOVA with Geisser-Greenhouse correction for unequal variance; 0.5 mg/kg: p = 0.0286; 1 mg/kg: p = 0.0286; 2 mg/kg: p = 0.0286; 4 mg/kg: p = 0.0191, Holm-Sidak post hoc test for multiple comparisons versus vehicle; Figure 2Biii).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of LFP data from 8 mice showing significant increases in low-gamma power at all CNO doses during running.

claim: CNO treatment did not significantly affect the percent of time spent running or mean running speed in hM3Dq-expressing mice.
source: We found no significant effect of treatment on locomotion (percent of time running: main effect of genotype: F(1, 10) = 0.1317, p = 0.7242; main effect of treatment: F(4, 40) = 0.5251, p = 0.7178; interaction: F(4, 40) = 1.265, p = 0.2996; running velocity: main effect of genotype: F(1, 10) = 0.2178, p = 0.6507); main effect of treatment: F(4, 40) = 0.1857; p = 0.9445); interaction: F(4, 40) = 0.8774, p = 0.4860; two-way ANOVA; Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of locomotor behavior showing no significant effects of CNO treatment.

claim: CNO administration significantly increased hippocampal low-gamma power during rest in hM3Dq-expressing Amigo2-icreERT2+ mice at doses of 1, 2, and 4 mg/kg.
source: Further, during periods of rest, we also found a significant increase in low-gamma power following CNO administration (F(2.306, 16.15) = 32.2, p < 0.0001, repeated-measures one-way ANOVA with Geisser-Greenhouse correction for unequal variance; 0.5 mg/kg: p = 0.1008; 1 mg/kg: p = 0.0161; 2 mg/kg: p = 0.0002; 4 mg/kg: p = 0.0004, Holm-Sidak post hoc test for multiple comparisons versus vehicle; Figure 2Ciii).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of LFP data from 8 mice showing significant increases in low-gamma power at 1, 2, and 4 mg/kg CNO doses during rest.

claim: CNO treatment did not significantly affect hippocampal high-gamma power during running in hM3Dq-expressing Amigo2-icreERT2+ mice.
source: High-gamma power was not significantly changed by CNO treatment compared with vehicle during either run (F(1.384, 9.69) = 2.288, p = 0.1602, repeated-measures one-way ANOVA with Geisser-Greenhouse correction for unequal variance, Figure 2Biv)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant effect of CNO on high-gamma power during running.

claim: CNO treatment did not significantly affect hippocampal high-gamma power during rest in hM3Dq-expressing Amigo2-icreERT2+ mice.
source: High-gamma power was not significantly changed by CNO treatment compared with vehicle during either run (F(1.384, 9.69) = 2.288, p = 0.1602, repeated-measures one-way ANOVA with Geisser-Greenhouse correction for unequal variance, Figure 2Biv) or rest (F(1.286, 9.003) = 4.775, p < 0.0501, repeated-measures one-way ANOVA with Geisser-Greenhouse correction for unequal variance, Figure 2Civ).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant effect of CNO on high-gamma power during rest.

claim: There was no significant difference in the magnitude of low-gamma power change between recordings from CA2, proximal CA1, and intermediate CA1 during periods of running or rest in hM3Dq-expressing mice.
source: We found no significant difference in the magnitude of low-gamma power change between recordings from close to CA2 and further from CA2 during periods of run (main effect of recording location: F(2, 5) = 0.6411, p = 0.5651; main effect of treatment: F(4, 20) = 6.668, p = 0.0014; interaction: F(8, 20) = 0.7554, p = 0.6443; Figure 2—figure supplement 6A–B) or periods of rest (main effect of location: F(2, 5) = 1.307, p = 0.3494; main effect of treatment: F(4, 20) = 29.98, p < 0.0001; interaction: F(8, 20) = 1.478, p = 2268; Figure 2—figure supplement 6C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis comparing low-gamma power changes across different recording locations.

claim: CNO treatment did not significantly affect theta phase at which low-gamma amplitude was greatest or modulation index in hM3Dq-expressing Amigo2-icreERT2+ mice.
source: We also measured theta phase, low-gamma amplitude comodulation during periods of running and found that neither theta phase at which low-gamma amplitude was greatest nor the modulation index was significantly affected by CNO treatment (N = 8, phase: F(1.266, 8.864) = 0.4696, p = 0.5552; modulation index: F(2.475, 17.33) = 3.11, p = 0.0612, repeated-measures one-way ANOVA with Geisser-Greenhouse correction for unequal variance; Figure 2—figure supplement 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of theta-gamma coupling showing no significant effects of CNO treatment.

claim: In control Amigo2-icreERT2- mice, CNO treatment had no effect on hippocampal low-gamma or high-gamma power during running.
source: In contrast, in control Amigo2-icreERT2- mice, during periods of running, CNO treatment had no effect on low- or high-gamma power (N = 4; low gamma: F(1.669, 5.006) = 1.36, p = 0.3281; high-gamma: F(1.895, 5.684) = 0.5079, p = 0.6175, repeated-measures one-way ANOVA with Geisser-Greenhouse correction for unequal variance; Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 5C–D, Figure 2—figure supplement 8)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of LFP data from 4 Cre-negative control mice showing no significant effects of CNO.

claim: CNO treatment significantly increased prefrontal cortical low-gamma power during both running and rest in hM3Dq-expressing Amigo2-icreERT2+ mice with on-target PFC electrode placement.
source: Using dual recordings from hippocampus and PFC, with implanted wire electrodes targeting prelimbic cortex (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1), we found that CNO treatment induced significant increases in low-gamma power in PFC during both run and rest periods (N = 4; run: F(1.177, 3.53) = 9.154, p = 0.0444; rest: (1.561, 4.6 84) =4.684, p = 0.0409, repeated-measures one-way ANOVA with Geisser-Greenhouse correction for unequal variance, Figure 3B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of PFC LFP data from 4 mice showing significant increases in low-gamma power during both running and rest.

claim: Control Amigo2-icreERT2- animals showed no significant change in PFC low-gamma power following CNO administration.
source: Control Amigo2-icreERT2- animals showed no significant change in PFC low-gamma power following CNO administration (N = 4; run: F(1.349, 4.047) = 1.809, p = 0.2617; Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of PFC LFP data from 4 Cre-negative control mice showing no significant effects of CNO.

claim: Amigo2-icreERT2+ animals with off-target PFC electrode placement showed no significant changes in low-gamma power despite showing increased hippocampal low-gamma power.
source: Further, we detected no significant changes in low-gamma power in Amigo2-icreERT2+ animals implanted with wire electrodes that missed their PFC target (N = 3; run: F(1.742, 3.483) = 0.7609, p = 0.5145; repeated-measures one-way ANOVA with Geisser-Greenhouse correction for unequal variance; Figure 3E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C; Figure 3—figure supplement 2) despite those animals showing increased low-gamma power in hippocampus (N = 3; F(1.39, 2.781) = 81.51, p = 0.0036; repeated-measures one-way ANOVA with Geisser-Greenhouse correction for unequal variance).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no PFC low-gamma changes in off-target recordings despite hippocampal changes.

claim: CNO administration significantly increased low-gamma coherence between hippocampus and PFC during both running and resting in hM3Dq-expressing Amigo2-icreERT2+ mice.
source: CNO administration produced a significant increase in low-gamma coherence between hippocampus and PFC during both run (N = 4; F(1.595, 4.786) = 8.279, p = 0.0305; repeated-measures one-way ANOVA with Geisser-Greenhouse correction for unequal variance; results of Holm-Sidak post hoc tests versus vehicle: 0.5 mg/kg: p = 0.5808, 1 mg/kg: p = 0.2079, 2 mg/kg: p = 0.0292, 4 mg/kg: p = 0.0292; Figure 3F), and rest (F(4, 12) = 11.71, p = 0.0004; repeated measured one-way ANOVA; results of Holm-Sidak post hoc tests versus vehicle: 0.5 mg/kg: p = 0.1189, 1 mg/kg: p = 0.1018, 2 mg/kg: p = 0.0006, 4 mg/kg: p = 0.0006; Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of coherence data from 4 mice showing significant increases during both running and rest.

claim: CNO treatment produced no significant change in coherence between hippocampus and PFC in control Amigo2-icreERT2- animals.
source: In contrast, treatment with CNO produced no significant change in coherence between hippocampus and PFC in control Amigo2-icreERT2- animals (N = 4; F(4, 12) = 1.053, p = 0.4209; repeated-measures one-way ANOVA; Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of coherence data from 4 Cre-negative control mice showing no significant effects of CNO.

claim: CNO administration (0.5 mg/kg) significantly decreased ripple event rate in hM3Dq-expressing Amigo2-icreERT2+ mice during rest.
source: In Amigo2-icreERT2+ animals, CNO administration significantly decreased ripple event rate relative to that observed following vehicle administration (N = 8; t(7) = 4.574, p = 0.0026; two-tailed paired t-test; Figure 4C)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of ripple data from 8 mice showing significant decrease in ripple event rate.

claim: CNO administration (0.5 mg/kg) did not significantly affect ripple amplitude in hM3Dq-expressing Amigo2-icreERT2+ mice.
source: although ripple amplitude was not significantly affected (t(7) = 0.3004, p = 0.7726; two-tailed paired t-test; Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant effect of CNO on ripple amplitude.

claim: In control Amigo2-icreERT2- animals, CNO administration had no effect on ripple event rate or amplitude.
source: In control Amigo2-icreERT2- animals, CNO administration had no effect on ripple event rate or amplitude (N = 4; event rate: t(3) = 1.871, p = 0.1581; amplitude: t(3) = 0.3193, p = 0.7704; two-tailed paired t-test; Figure 4E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of ripple data from 4 Cre-negative control mice showing no significant effects of CNO.

claim: hM4Di reduced CA2 synaptic output to CA1, with inhibition detected as early as 20 minutes post-CNO treatment and lasting for at least 4 hours.
source: Optogenetic stimulation of CA2 in these awake, behaving animals evoked detectable voltage responses in CA1 that were inhibited as early as 20 min post CNO treatment (the earliest we tested). In this preparation, we detected inhibition of CA2 responses for 4 hr. By 24 hr, responses recovered to 77.20% of pre-CNO response amplitude (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic stimulation data showing time course of hM4Di-mediated inhibition, as shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: CNO administration (5 mg/kg) significantly decreased hippocampal low-gamma power during running in hM4Di-expressing Amigo2-icreERT2+ mice.
source: We found a significant decrease in low-gamma power during running following CNO administration compared with vehicle (t(7) = 4.408, p = 0.0031, two-tailed paired t-test, Figure 5Aiii, Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of LFP data from 8 mice showing significant decrease in low-gamma power during running.

claim: There was no significant difference in the magnitude of low-gamma power change between recordings from dorsal CA1 and intermediate CA1 during periods of running or rest in hM4Di-expressing mice.
source: We again found a main effect of drug treatment during periods of running but no significant difference in the magnitude of low-gamma power change between recordings from dorsal CA1 and recordings from intermediate CA1 during periods of running (main effect of treatment: F(1, 6) = 17.84, p = 0.0055; main effect of location: F(1, 6) = 1.002, p = 0.3555; interaction: F(1, 6) = 0.428, p = 0.5372; Figure 5—figure supplement 3A–B) or periods of rest (main effect of treatment: F(1, 6) = 0.3002, p = 0.6035; main effect of location: F(1, 6) = 0.2614, p = 0.6274; interaction: F(1, 6) = 4.278, p = 0.0841; Figure 5—figure supplement 3C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis comparing low-gamma power changes across different recording locations.

claim: CNO treatment did not significantly affect the percent of time spent running or mean running speed in hM4Di-expressing mice.
source: We found no difference in either of these measures (percent of time running: main effect of genotype: F(1, 12) = 0.02054, p = 0.8884; main effect of treatment: (1, 12) = 2.988; interaction (F(1, 12) = 0.02761, p = 0.8708; running velocity: main effect of genotype: F(1, 12) = 0.2934, p = 0.5979; main effect of treatment: F(1, 12) = 2.465, p = 0.1424; interaction: (F(1, 12) = 0.02162, p = 0.8855; two-way ANOVA; Figure 2—figure supplement 4C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of locomotor behavior showing no significant effects of CNO treatment.

claim: CNO treatment significantly decreased modulation index but not theta phase of peak gamma amplitude in hM4Di-expressing Amigo2-icreERT2+ mice.
source: We also measured theta phase, low-gamma amplitude comodulation during periods of running and found that theta phase of peak gamma amplitude was not significantly affected by CNO but modulation index was significantly decreased with CNO treatment (N = 8, phase: t(7) = 1.000, p = 0.3506, two-tailed paired t-test; modulation index: W = -32, p = 0.0234, Wilcoxon signed-ranked test; Figure 5—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of theta-gamma coupling showing significant decrease in modulation index but not phase.

claim: CNO treatment did not significantly affect hippocampal theta or high-gamma power during running in hM4Di-expressing Amigo2-icreERT2+ mice.
source: Treatment with CNO did not affect theta or high-gamma power during running (theta: t(7) = 0.7786, p = 0.4617; high-gamma: t(7) = 2.029, p = 0.0821)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant effects of CNO on theta or high-gamma power during running.

claim: CNO treatment did not significantly affect hippocampal theta, low-gamma, or high-gamma power during rest in hM4Di-expressing Amigo2-icreERT2+ mice.
source: and did not affect power in any of these frequency bands during periods of rest (theta: t(7) = 2.214, p = 0.0625; low-gamma: (t(7) = 0.4522, p = 0.6648; high-gamma: t(7) = 0.172, p = 0.8683; Figure 5A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant effects of CNO on any frequency band during rest.

claim: CA2 pyramidal neurons possess axons that primarily target CA1, with most fluorescently-labeled CA2 axons targeting stratum oriens in intermediate CA1.
source: CA2 pyramidal neurons have been shown to possess axons with large rostral to caudal trajectories, primarily targeting CA1 (Tamamaki et al., 1988). Consistent with a projection toward caudal CA1, we observed fluorescence from hM4Di-mCherry+ axon fibers in caudal intermediate CA1, with most of the fluorescently-labeled CA2 axons targeting stratum oriens in CA1 (Kohara et al., 2014) (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical data showing mCherry-labeled axons in CA1 stratum oriens and cited literature (Tamamaki et al., 1988; Kohara et al., 2014).

claim: Inhibition of CA2 pyramidal neurons decreased PFC low-gamma power during running in hM4Di-expressing Amigo2-icreERT2+ mice.
source: In Amigo2-icreERT2+ mice, we observed a small but consistent decrease in PFC low-gamma power during running following CNO administration compared with vehicle (N = 6; t(5) = 2.948, p = 0.0320; two-tailed paired t-test; Figure 5D)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of PFC LFP data from 6 mice showing significant decrease in low-gamma power during running.

claim: CNO treatment did not significantly affect PFC theta or high-gamma power in hM4Di-expressing Amigo2-icreERT2+ mice.
source: We found no change in PFC theta or high gamma power (theta: t(5) = 1.341, p = 0.2375; high gamma: t(5) = 0.738, p = 0.4937, paired t-test; Figure 5Diii).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant effects of CNO on PFC theta or high-gamma power.

claim: Control Amigo2-icreERT2- animals showed no significant change in hippocampal or PFC low-gamma power in response to CNO treatment in hM4Di experiments.
source: Control Amigo2-icreERT2- animals showed no significant change in hippocampal or PFC low-gamma power in response to CNO treatment compared with vehicle (N = 5; hippocampus: t(4) = 1.079, p = 0.3413, two-tailed paired t-test; PFC: t(4) = 0.4293, p = 0.6898, two-tailed paired t-test; Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 5C–D)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of LFP data from 5 Cre-negative control mice showing no significant effects of CNO.

claim: CNO administration (5 mg/kg) significantly increased ripple event rate in hM4Di-expressing Amigo2-icreERT2+ mice during rest.
source: As predicted based on our findings in hM3Dq-infused animals, CNO administration significantly increased ripple event rate in hM4Di-infused animals (N = 6; t(5) = 3.809, p = 0.0063; one-tailed paired t-test; Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of ripple data from 6 mice showing significant increase in ripple event rate.

claim: CNO administration (5 mg/kg) significantly increased ripple amplitude in hM4Di-expressing Amigo2-icreERT2+ mice.
source: CNO administration also increased ripple amplitude in hM4Di animals (t(p = 0.0278; two-tailed paired t-test; Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing significant increase in ripple amplitude.

claim: In control Amigo2-icreERT2- mice, CNO administration did not significantly change ripple event rate or amplitude in hM4Di experiments.
source: By contrast, in control Amigo2-icreERT2- mice, CNO administration did not significantly change ripple event rate or amplitude (N = 6; event rate: W = 5, p = 0.6875, Wilcoxon signed-ranked test; amplitude: t(5) = 0.5165, p = 0.6275, two-tailed paired t-test; Figure 6E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of ripple data from 6 Cre-negative control mice showing no significant effects of CNO.

claim: High-gamma oscillations in CA1 are prevalent in stratum lacunosum-moleculare and co-occur with high-gamma oscillations in medial entorhinal cortex.
source: High-gamma (~60 – 100 Hz) oscillations in CA1 are prevalent in stratum lacunosum-moleculare (Schomburg et al., 2014), co-occur with high-gamma oscillations in medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) (Colgin et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Schomburg et al., 2014; Colgin et al., 2009).

claim: High-gamma oscillations are increased by Gq-DREADD-mediated activation of cortex.
source: are increased by Gq-Designer Receptors Exclusively Activated by Designer Drugs (DREADD)-mediated activation of cortex (Alexander et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Alexander et al., 2009).

claim: High-gamma oscillations are impaired by lesioning of entorhinal cortex.
source: and are impaired by lesioning of EC (Bragin et al., 1995), leading to the conclusion that high-gamma oscillations arise from MEC.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Bragin et al., 1995) and inference about the source of high-gamma oscillations.

claim: High-gamma power is increased upon exploration of novel stimuli.
source: High-gamma is thought to contribute to memory encoding because high-gamma power is increased upon exploration of novel stimuli (Zheng et al., 2016; Kemere et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Zheng et al., 2016; Kemere et al., 2013).

claim: Low-gamma oscillations in CA1 are prevalent in stratum radiatum and synchronize with low-gamma in CA3.
source: Low-gamma (~30 – 55 Hz) oscillations in CA1 are prevalent in stratum radiatum (Schomburg et al., 2014), synchronize with low-gamma in CA3 (Colgin, 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Schomburg et al., 2014; Colgin, 2015).

claim: Low-gamma oscillations become more evident upon entorhinal cortex lesioning.
source: and become more evident upon EC lesioning (Bragin et al., 1995), supporting the conclusion that low-gamma oscillations arise from CA3.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Bragin et al., 1995) and inference about the source of low-gamma oscillations.

claim: The magnitude of low-gamma coupling to theta oscillations correlates with performance on learned behavioral tasks.
source: Low-gamma oscillations are believed to promote memory retrieval because the magnitude of low-gamma coupling to theta oscillations correlates with performance on learned behavioral tasks (Tort et al., 2009; Shirvalkar et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Tort et al., 2009; Shirvalkar et al., 2010).

claim: Complete silencing of CA3 synaptic output with tetanus toxin light chain does not completely impair low-gamma oscillations.
source: Interestingly, complete silencing of the synaptic output of CA3 with tetanus toxin light chain does not completely impair low-gamma oscillations (Middleton and McHugh, 2016), suggesting the presence of another source of low-gamma oscillations.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Middleton and McHugh, 2016) and inference about additional sources of low-gamma.

claim: Sharp-wave ripples are high frequency (~100 – 250 Hz), short-duration electrical events prominently seen in LFP recordings from CA1 during awake immobility and slow wave sleep.
source: Another prominent oscillation seen in hippocampus is sharp-wave ripple oscillations, which are high frequency (~100 – 250 Hz), short-duration electrical events prominently seen in LFP recordings from CA1 during awake immobility and slow wave sleep (Buzsáki et al., 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Buzsáki et al., 1992).

claim: Sharp waves are thought to arise from the synchronous firing of CA3 pyramidal cells, which depolarize the apical dendrites of CA1 pyramidal cells.
source: Sharp waves are thought to arise from the synchronous firing of CA3 pyramidal cells, which depolarize the apical dendrites of CA1 pyramidal cells. The synchronous CA3 firing recruits excitatory and inhibitory neurons in CA1 to generate ripples (Buzsáki et al., 1992; Ylinen et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Buzsáki et al., 1992; Ylinen et al., 1995).

claim: Kay et al. (2016) found that CA2 is the only hippocampal subregion to have a substantial population of neurons that cease firing during ripples.
source: found that CA2 is the only hippocampal subregion to have a substantial population of neurons that cease firing during ripples (termed 'N cells'), whereas nearly all pyramidal cells queried in neighboring subfields fired during ripples. Although not associated with ripples, these N cells fired at high rates during low running speed or immobility (Kay et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Kay et al., 2016).

claim: Oliva et al. (2016) reported that CA2 pyramidal cell activity ramps up before the onset of sharp-wave ripples.
source: Oliva et al. (2016) later reported that CA2 pyramidal cell activity ramps up before the onset of sharp-wave ripples, leading these authors to conclude that CA2 neurons play a leading role in ripple generation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Oliva et al., 2016).

claim: Boehringer et al. (2017) found that chronic silencing of CA2 pyramidal cell output leads to the occurrence of epileptic discharges arising from CA3.
source: By contrast, Boehringer et al. (2017) later found that chronic silencing of CA2 pyramidal cell output leads to the occurrence of epileptic discharges arising from CA3, which the authors suggested reflect anomalous ripple oscillations.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Boehringer et al., 2017).

claim: Area CA2 has been recognized for its role in processing long-term memories containing socially relevant information in rodents.
source: Area CA2 has recently been recognized for its role in processing long-term memories containing socially relevant information in rodents (Alexander et al., 2016; Hitti and Siegelbaum, 2014; Pagani et al., 2015; Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Alexander et al., 2016; Hitti and Siegelbaum, 2014; Pagani et al., 2015; Smith et al., 2016).

claim: A mouse model of schizophrenia that shows hypoactive CA2 pyramidal cells in vitro also shows impaired social behavior.
source: Interestingly, a mouse model of schizophrenia that shows hypoactive CA2 pyramidal cells in vitro also shows impaired social behavior (Piskorowski et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Piskorowski et al., 2016).

claim: Long-range synchrony between hippocampus and prefrontal cortex, including low-gamma coherence, is impaired in a mouse model of schizophrenia.
